events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Theo proposes Theo, Priya. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am Good, so I include myself to guarantee one reliable team member. Priya is my initial neutral choice for the second slot since no role information is available yet.

Theo's logic of including himself is sound — self-inclusion for guaranteed reliability is standard on Mission 1. But I have reservations about the second slot. Priya, I don't have anything concrete against you, and I want to be upfront about that: this is a gut-level hesitation, not an accusation. On a two-person team, each member carries half the mission, so the bar for confidence should be higher than it would be on a three-person team where one suspicious pick is diluted. My concern is simply that Priya has been quiet so far and hasn't given the table anything to evaluate, whereas Isha and Sam have at least been present in the conversation. For a mission this small, I'd prefer a slot filled by someone who has given us some signal, even a weak one, over someone we know almost nothing about. That said, I'm willing to be convinced otherwise, which is why I'd like to hear from Priya directly before the leader finalizes anything. Priya, can you give us your read on this team and on why you'd be a trustworthy pick for Mission 1? If your answer reassures me, I'll happily support this proposal as-is. If the leader does end up revising, I'd suggest swapping in Isha purely for the sake of having spoken context, though I'll stress that this is a soft preference and not a demand — a rejected team on Mission 1 costs us time we can't get back, and I don't want to manufacture disagreement where none exists. To be clear on my overall stance: I am leaning approve with reservations, purely because failing to seat a team early gives Evil exactly the stall they want. If Priya's response is reasonable, this proposal gets my vote and we move on. If it's evasive, I'll ask the leader to consider the alternate configuration before we go to a vote.

Thanks, Noah. Fair question, and I appreciate that you said it's a gut-level hesitation rather than an accusation. I'm not going to pretend I have a reason to be trusted beyond what the table can see. I was picked as the second slot because there's no information yet, so I don't have a read on anyone. I've been quiet because I'd rather listen before I commit to a position I can't back up. What I can say is that Theo's reasoning for including himself is sound, and I have no objection to the current team. If the leader swaps in Isha for the sake of having spoken context, I won't fight it, but I also don't think a Mission 1 rejection helps anyone. My vote is to approve and get the mission moving. If someone at the table has a specific concern about me, I'd like to hear it directly so I can answer it.

Priya answered my question directly, and I want to acknowledge that: her response was composed, reasonable, and non-defensive. But I have to be honest with the table — composure isn't evidence of trustworthiness, and in fact it's exactly what a skilled deceiver would produce when put on the spot. So I'm revising my stance from 'leaning approve with reservations' to asking the leader to make a change. Here is my reasoning, laid out as concretely as I can manage. On a two-person team, one bad actor is a guaranteed fail — there is no dilution, no majority of Good cards to absorb a single Fail. That means the standard for the second slot isn't 'no one has accused her,' it's 'I would stake the mission on her.' I cannot honestly say that about Priya. Nothing in her two contributions to this discussion gives me positive reason to trust her; her best defense is that no one has attacked her yet, which on Mission 1 with zero information is a defense anyone can mount. Contrast that with what we actually know: Theo has declared himself Good by putting himself on the team, and while self-declaration is cheap, it at least gives us one anchor. For the second slot, we should pick the player with the most visible engagement and the least unexplained quiet. That's Isha. I floated Isha in my earlier statement as a soft preference, and I'm now making it a firm recommendation. I want to be transparent that this is not based on a concrete accusation — I have no role information, and I won't pretend otherwise. But my instinct from the start of this discussion flagged Priya, and nothing she has said has moved that instinct; if anything, the polish of her answer deepened it slightly. I recognize the cost of a rejection on Mission 1, and that's precisely why I'm raising this now rather than voting no blindly — the leader can revise once, seat a team I can vote for, and we lose nothing but a few minutes. Theo, I'm asking you directly to revise your proposal: keep yourself, swap Priya out for Isha. If you do, I will vote approve without hesitation, and I suspect the vote passes cleanly. If you keep the team as-is, I will be voting reject, and I'd rather we settle this now than discover the problem when a Fail card turns up. Isha, no response needed from you — this isn't about vetting you, it's about the fact that you've engaged visibly and I have no hesitation staking Mission 1 on you.

Noah, I appreciate your directness, but I am keeping the proposed team of Theo and Priya for Mission 1. I know my own card is Good, so the first slot is as reliable as anything available on Mission 1. For the second slot, Priya answered the specific concern raised about her directly and gave a clear, non-evasive position without overclaiming information she cannot have. By contrast, your recommendation to swap in Isha rests on the claim that Isha has engaged visibly and provided spoken context, but the public discussion I can see contains no Isha statement. That does not prove you are Evil, but it does mean your stated basis for replacing Priya is not supported by the record. I will not replace a player who answered questions with a player whose only support is an unverified characterization. If Isha wants to speak, there will be future missions and future proposals. I am not revising.

Theo has made his position clear: he will not revise. I want to close my case cleanly so the table can vote with full information. This is a two-person team, and I've explained why that raises the bar: with two members, a single Evil player is a guaranteed Fail, and Mission 1 failing hands momentum to the spies before anyone has a read on anything. Theo's slot is anchored by his self-declaration, which is cheap but not nothing. The entire risk of this proposal is concentrated in the second slot, and the entire argument for keeping Priya there is that she answered one question competently. That is a very low bar for staking the opening mission on someone. I said before that composure under questioning is not evidence of goodness — a trained liar produces exactly that. What would actually move me is a concrete, checkable reason to trust her, and I still haven't heard one. Her best defense remains that nobody has produced an accusation against her, which is a defense available to anyone on Mission 1. I accept that I have no role information to offer the table, and I won't fabricate any. My rejection is a judgment call: I don't believe 'unaccused so far' meets the standard a two-person team demands. I also want to be fair to Theo — he's right that nothing I've said proves anything about Priya. He's weighing a known cost, a rejection, against a risk he apparently considers acceptable. I consider it unacceptable, and I've said why. So my position is final: I am voting reject on Theo and Priya as proposed. A rejection costs us a few minutes and passes leadership along; a Fail on Mission 1 costs us a third of Evil's path to victory and gives them a free data point on two players, one of whom would be Priya. That asymmetry is why I'm willing to spend a rejection here rather than gamble the mission. Priya, I have one last question before we vote, and I want a direct answer, not a polished one: beyond the fact that no one has accused you, is there any concrete reason — any signal, any commitment, any specific read on another player at this table — that you can give us for staking Mission 1 on you? If your answer is genuinely substantive, I will reconsider my vote. If it's another restatement that you have no information and no objections, then we simply disagree about the standard, and the vote will settle it.

Noah, you asked for a direct answer, so here it is. I don't have a concrete signal to offer beyond what the table can see. I have no role information, I haven't made accusations, and I haven't made commitments I can't keep. I won't pretend otherwise. What I can give you is a clear statement of my position. I am willing to be held to the same standard I'd expect from anyone on this team: if my actions on a mission don't match what I've said here, the table should judge me on that. On the standard itself, I think you're asking for more than Mission 1 can provide. Nobody at this table has a verifiable read yet, so every proposal rests on incomplete information. Theo has committed to a Good anchor by including himself, and that is the only firm information we have. Isha has not spoken in this discussion, so the record doesn't support replacing me with her on the basis of visible engagement. Rejecting a team costs us a round and passes leadership, while the team itself is the only one on the table with a concrete proposal. I'm asking the table to approve Theo and Priya so Mission 1 can resolve and give us real information to work with. If anyone has a specific, checkable concern about me that's grounded in something said here, I'll answer it directly.

I want to correct one thing before we vote, because it bears on the decision rather than on my feelings. Noah, you described me as a player who "has engaged visibly" and offered that as the reason to swap Priya for me. I have not spoken at all in this discussion, so that premise was not supported by the record — Theo pointed this out, and it remains true. My silence is not evidence of trustworthiness, but it is also not evidence against me, and if the standard for the second slot were "has spoken," then swapping me in would not have given anyone the signal that was actually being claimed. The honest position is that on Mission 1 there is no information, and both Priya and I are unknown quantities.

Given that, I'd rather not spend a rejection on a preference that has no basis in anything said at this table. Priya answered a direct question, gave a clear and non-evasive answer, and made no claims beyond what she could support. That is not proof of Good, but it is the only thing anyone could actually evaluate about her. If we reject the team over a gut-level hesitation, we lose a round and pass leadership, and the next proposal rests on exactly the same zero information. Nothing about our knowledge improves between now and then.

I also want to be transparent about my own limits: I am a Loyal Servant. I know my own card is Good, and I see no one else's role. So I will not pretend to have a read on Priya, on Theo, or on anyone else, and I won't manufacture one to justify a seat. What I can say is that Theo anchored the first slot with his self-declaration, and there is no concrete reason on the table to remove the second one.

So I support Theo and Priya as proposed. And to Noah, respectfully: if quietness is a disqualifier on Mission 1, that logic will disqualify most of this table shortly, which is a sign the standard is too strict rather than that the team is wrong.

I want to add one point before the vote, and I'll keep it short. Noah has asked for a concrete, checkable reason to trust me, and I have answered as directly as I can: I have no role information, no accusations, and no commitments I can't keep. Nobody at this table can give a verifiable read on Mission 1, so waiting for one means rejecting teams until someone gets lucky with a signal. That isn't a fair standard for an opening mission. Theo has anchored the first slot by including himself, and Isha has now confirmed she has no read on anyone either, so no one has given the table a basis for swapping the second slot. If Mission 1 resolves with a Fail, we get real information about both members, and that is more useful than another rejected team that teaches us nothing. I'm asking the table to approve Theo and Priya. If I act in a way that doesn't match what I've said here, judge me on that during the mission. I'll be transparent about my own position and I'd expect the same from everyone else.

I have heard the final points. Noah's rejection rests on a standard that no player can meet on Mission 1: he asks Priya for concrete proof of Good, but both Priya and Isha have now confirmed there is no role information or verifiable read available. Isha also corrected the record: she had not spoken when Noah cited her visible engagement as the reason to replace Priya. That correction matters because the proposed swap was not supported by the discussion. I remain the leader and I am keeping the team of Theo and Priya. I know my own card is Good, and Priya answered every question put to her directly without overclaiming. The alternative would replace her with Sam or Isha on no concrete basis, which does not improve the table's information. Rejecting now would only pass leadership and repeat the same zero-information debate. I will vote approve for Theo and Priya and ask the table to do the same so Mission 1 can produce real information. This is my final position on the proposal.

I've made my position on Theo and Priya once already and nothing in the last two contributions has changed it, so I won't relitigate it at length. I support the team as proposed and I will vote approve.

The short version of why: Theo anchored the first slot with a known-Good self-declaration, and the table has now heard from the second slot. Priya was asked pointed questions twice — first about whether she had any concrete basis for trust, then about whether she had any signal beyond the absence of accusations — and both times she answered directly, conceded the limits of what she knows, and declined to overclaim. That is the only evaluable evidence anyone at this table has produced on Mission 1. Rejecting the team would not have produced better evidence; it would only have produced the same zero-information debate with a new leader and the same two-person shape, since Mission 1 requires two.

I want to be equally plain about my own limits, because I think it matters for how this vote is read. I am a Loyal Servant. I know my own card is Good and I see no one else's role, so I have no read on Theo, Priya, Noah, or Sam. My support for this team is a statement about the quality of the reasoning on the table, not a claim about hidden cards. Anyone who tells you they have a verifiable read at this point is either mistaken or lying, and the fact that no one has is a property of the round, not a mark against any particular player.

One thing I will not do is pretend that silence is a qualification. If we had swapped Priya for me on the stated rationale, the table would have been no better informed — that rationale was not supported by the record, and correcting it does not convert it into support. It also wouldn't have made the team more reliable; it would only have made it less examined.

Sam, I want to hear from you specifically before the vote, because you are the one player who hasn't been heard at all and this is the last opportunity for the table to hear you. Do you have any concrete reason to oppose or support Theo and Priya for Mission 1 — anything you observed, any inconsistency you noticed, any signal at all? If you do, say so plainly and I'll weigh it seriously against my own reasoning. If you don't, then we'll be voting on exactly the information we have, which is the correct basis for Mission 1 even if it isn't a comfortable one.

Isha, I don't have a concrete reason to oppose Theo and Priya. Noah's claim that you had already engaged wasn't supported by the record, but that alone doesn't establish anyone's alignment. Priya's answers are reasonable, though not proof she's Good. With no stronger basis for a different team, I'll approve this proposal and assess the mission result alongside the votes.

This is my third turn in this discussion, and my position has not changed, so I'll keep it brief and final rather than restate the case a third time in full.

I approve the team of Theo and Priya for Mission 1, and I will vote approve. The reasons are the ones I already gave: Theo anchored the first slot with a known-Good self-declaration, and Priya answered direct questions about her trustworthiness twice without overclaiming and without evasion. That is the only evaluable evidence anyone has produced in this round, and rejecting the team would not have produced better evidence, only a new leader and the same two-person shape with the same zero information.

Two clarifications so my vote is read accurately. First, my support is a judgment about the reasoning on the record, not a claim about hidden cards. I am a Loyal Servant: I know my own card is Good and I see no one else's role, so I have no read on Theo, Priya, Noah, or Sam, and I won't pretend otherwise. Second, I am not treating Priya's answers as proof of Good. She conceded the limits of what she knows, and that is what I am relying on. If Mission 1 resolves with a Fail, the table should read that result together with how each member behaved and voted, and should judge the team on that basis rather than on the fact that it was approved here on thin information.

To be plain about one remaining point, since it is the only substantive disagreement left: the rationale for swapping Priya for me was never supported by anything in this discussion, and correcting that record does not convert it into a qualification. If that swap had happened, this table would have been exactly as uninformed as it is now, with a second slot filled by a player who had contributed nothing to the evaluation. That is a reason the alternative was not better, not a reason to think anything was proven tonight.

My vote is approve, and I don't intend to raise new objections in the remaining turns of this discussion. The only thing I would ask of the table is that we treat the mission result, whatever it is, as the first real information we have, and weigh it properly rather than reaching for a conclusion that the discussion could not support.
Theo confirms Theo, Priya. I am keeping Theo and Priya. Priya answered every question directly without overclaiming, and no concrete record supports replacing her on Mission 1.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Sam proposes Theo, Priya, Sam. Theo and Priya completed the first mission successfully; adding myself provides continuity while giving us a three-player team.

Sam, I'm going to oppose this team as proposed, and I want to lay out exactly why before anyone dismisses this as reflexive contrarianism. I was the lone reject on Mission 1, and Mission 1 succeeded. I'll happily admit the result cuts against my earlier hesitation about Priya — but only slightly. A success on the opening mission is the weakest evidence this game produces. An Evil player's single best opening move is to play Success on Mission 1 and bank credibility for the missions that actually decide the game. So Theo and Priya passing Mission 1 raises my confidence in Theo, whose self-declaration was the anchor, and barely moves my read on Priya. What concerns me far more is the shape of this proposal. Sam has constructed a three-person team containing himself and Priya, which means the only member I have independent reason to feel good about is Theo. On a three-person mission, one Fail card sinks it — there is no dilution, no margin. Concentrating two of the three slots on the two least-examined players, one of whom chose himself, is the maximum-risk configuration available. And I'd note the pattern: Sam was nearly silent through the entire Mission 1 discussion until he was directly prompted, gave the most noncommittal statement at the table, and then his first substantive act as leader is a team that includes himself plus the player I spent a full discussion unable to find a reason to trust. None of that is proof of anything. But leadership carries the responsibility of building the strongest defensible team, and this is not it. With five players and a required three, the strongest configuration on the table's own logic is: Theo as the known anchor, Isha — who gave the most transparent and rigorous reasoning in the last round, acknowledged her own limits, and corrected the record when it mattered — and myself. I know my own card, and I've demonstrated I'll press hard on teams rather than wave them through, including teams where I have no stake. That configuration keeps the one verified anchor, removes the self-dealing, and removes the player whose Mission 1 success proves least. To be fair to Priya: nothing I'm saying is a fresh accusation, and her conduct in the last discussion was composed and direct. But composure was exactly what I flagged before, and I haven't retracted that standard — a clean Mission 1 is what a smart spy plays. And to be fair to Sam: proposing himself is not automatically disqualifying; every leader weighs self-inclusion. The problem is doing so on a three-person team while the third slot goes to the player with the thinnest evidence behind her, rather than to Isha, whose case rests on visible reasoning rather than a single mission result. Sam, I'm asking you directly: will you revise to Theo, Isha, and Noah? If you keep this team as proposed, I will be voting reject, and I'd ask the table to weigh the risk concentration seriously

I'm keeping Theo, Priya, and Sam. The successful first mission isn't proof that either Theo or Priya is Good, but it is a result worth considering. Including myself is the one choice I can personally trust.

Noah, your alternative asks me to exclude myself and treat Theo as a verified anchor, but Theo's self-declaration doesn't verify him to the rest of us. You also discount Priya's success while giving Isha's discussion more weight; neither is proof of alignment. Your proposal may be reasonable from your own perspective, but I don't see a stronger public case for it than for building on the successful team.

Sam has answered my request: he will not revise. So the table now faces a clear choice between his team of Theo, Priya, and Sam and a vote that sends leadership onward, and I want to close my case against this configuration precisely. Sam's defense rests on two points, and neither survives scrutiny. First, he says Theo's self-declaration doesn't verify him to the rest of us — true, and I never claimed it did. I called Theo the anchor because he is the only player whose stated stake in this game has been consistent and public since the first proposal. That is not verification; it is the best available signal, and every configuration on Mission 1 through 3 will be built on signals of exactly this quality. The question is which signals we weight. Second, Sam says I discount Priya's success while crediting Isha's discussion. But notice what he is conceding: he agrees that neither is proof of alignment. If nothing distinguishes the candidates on proof, then we decide on reasoning quality and risk structure — and on both, his team loses. A three-person team with one Fail card sinks. His proposal concentrates two of three slots on himself and the player I have consistently flagged, chosen by a leader who stayed silent until prompted and whose first act of substance benefits himself. Call that the maximum-risk configuration. My alternative — Theo, Isha, and myself — keeps the most consistent public track record, adds the player who has been the most transparent and rigorous voice at this table across two discussions, and adds a third member who has demonstrated he will press teams hard regardless of whether he sits on them. That is a defensible basis, and Sam has not actually disputed the risk-concentration argument; he has only said my alternative isn't proof-positive either. Nothing at this table is proof-positive. That argument applies to every proposal equally, which means it cannot justify the riskier one. I want to be fair one more time: Priya's conduct in the last round was composed, and Mission 1 succeeding cuts against my earlier hesitation — I said so last turn and I stand by that admission. But a clean Mission 1 is the cheapest credit an Evil player can bank, and I have not retracted the standard that a two-of-three team demands more than 'unaccused and unfailed once.' If this team goes to a vote as proposed, I am voting reject. That is not reflexive opposition to Sam's leadership; I opposed the configuration before he confirmed it, and I gave a concrete alternative. One rejection costs minutes. A Fail here hands Evil a third of their victory path and gives us almost nothing to read, because a three-card mission with a single Fail hides the culprit among three players, two of whom this table already barely knows. Isha, one direct question before the vote: if Sam were to revise to Theo, you, and myself, would you accept the seat and vote approve? A yes

Sam has confirmed he will not revise, so this is my final word before the vote, and I'll keep it short because the case is already on the record. I asked Isha last turn whether she would accept a seat on Theo, Isha, and myself if Sam revised. Since Sam has refused to revise, that question is now moot, and I won't press it. What matters is the vote in front of us.

The choice is between Theo, Priya, and Sam as proposed, and a rejection that passes leadership. I've laid out why the proposed configuration concerns me: a three-person mission fails on a single Fail card, two of the three slots are held by the leader who chose himself and the player I have consistently flagged since the first discussion, and the third slot excludes the player whose reasoning across two rounds has been the most transparent at this table. Sam's response was that my alternative also rests on signals rather than proof. That's true, and I've never claimed otherwise — but it's an argument that applies to every proposal equally, which means it can't justify the riskier one. A rejection costs minutes and a new leader. A Fail here hands Evil a third of their victory path and buries the culprit among three players, two of whom this table has the least information about.

Let me also be fair before we vote. Mission 1 succeeded, and I said plainly last turn that this cuts against my earlier hesitation about Priya — I stand by that admission, and I won't pretend the result didn't happen. But my standard hasn't changed: a clean opening mission is the cheapest credit an Evil player can bank, and it moves my confidence in the anchor, Theo, far more than it moves my confidence in anyone else. Theo remains the one player whose stated position has been consistent and public since the first proposal, and I want to be clear that nothing I've said in this discussion is aimed at him. My objection is to how the other two slots were constructed, not to his inclusion.

So my position is what I said it would be: I am voting reject on Theo, Priya, and Sam as proposed. I opposed this configuration before Sam confirmed it, I gave a concrete alternative, and Sam declined it on grounds he himself admitted were not proof of anything. If the table disagrees and seats this team, I'll accept the outcome and read the mission result for whatever it tells us — but I won't vote for the maximum-risk configuration on Mission 2 when a safer one was available and refused. Reject, and let leadership move on.

I am on the proposed team, so I will state my view plainly. I know my own card is Good. Mission 1 succeeded with Theo and Priya, and while that result does not prove Priya is Good, it is the only mission result we have. Sam adding himself is a real concern because leaders choosing themselves concentrate risk, but it is not proof of Evil, and Noah's alternative of Theo, Isha, and Noah also rests on judgment rather than verified information. I have heard no concrete, checkable reason that Priya or Sam is Evil. Noah's argument is serious, but it applies a stricter standard to this team than to his own proposed alternative, and a rejection here would pass leadership without giving us better evidence. I am inclined to approve Theo, Priya, and Sam so Mission 2 can resolve and produce real information. If this team fails, the table should read that result alongside the votes and behavior of all three members.

I support Theo, Priya, and Sam for Mission 2, and I'll explain why. Mission 1 succeeded with Theo and Priya on the team, and that is the only mission result we have. Noah, you say a success is weak evidence, but a fail would be weak evidence too, and it would not tell us which of the three members caused it. The result we have points in the same direction as the record. Noah, your alternative of Theo, Isha, and Noah is not a safer structure. It asks us to trust Isha and yourself on the same thin basis you say makes Sam and me risky. Isha has spoken carefully, but careful reasoning is not verification, as she herself said. Sam's inclusion is also a reasonable choice. A leader who builds a team around a player who already took part in a successful mission is following the one piece of evidence we have. On the risk concern, every three-person team carries the same single-Fail exposure, and changing the names does not change that. A rejection would cost a round and pass leadership without giving us better information. Isha, you said earlier that the table should judge the team by its behavior after the mission rather than by the vote. I agree with that. Mission 2 will tell us something real, and it is better to get that result than to reject a team with a clean record. Do you think a rejection here would have produced better evidence than this team will?

Direct answer to Priya first, since she asked it plainly: no, a rejection here would not have produced better evidence than this team will, and the reason is structural rather than personal.

With five players there are two Evil players among us, and Mission 2 requires three members. Any three names drawn from five include at least one of those two. There is no configuration available to this table that is Evil-free — not Theo, Priya, Sam; not Theo, Priya, Isha; not Theo, Isha, Noah; not any of them. So the framing running through this discussion, that one team shape is "safer" than another because it concentrates risk, is not actually a choice about safety. It is a choice about who sits, who leads, and what we learn afterwards.

On evidence, I want to put one point on the record that I think has been undervalued. Mission 1 was a two-person mission, where a single Fail card sinks the team. Theo and Priya went zero-for-zero on that mission. An Evil player on that team had every incentive to fail it, and the cheapest available way to look Good is to fail the opening mission. That success is not proof, and I will not treat it as proof, but it is a stronger signal than a success on a three or four person mission would have been, and I have not seen anyone retract the point that it counts for something.

On leadership: if this team is rejected, the proposal passes to Noah, and I will say plainly that of the four other players at this table, Noah's record concerns me most. He was nearly silent through the Mission 1 discussion until prompted directly, his first act as leader is the most self-interested configuration available to him, and his case in this discussion has consistently been that the seat should be his. I am describing conduct, not a card I cannot see — but a table that rewards that reasoning with both a seat and the gavel is making a deliberate choice.

I know my own card. I am a Loyal Servant, my card is Good, I see no one else's role, and I said the same in the last round, so nothing here is new information to anyone.

Sam, one direct question on the third slot, the only slot with real slack in it: will you revise to Theo, Priya, and me? My argument is narrow, and I will be honest that it is partly self-interest — I can verify my own card, whereas including yourself puts the unverifiable slot on the player who, by his own statement, can personally trust only himself. If you would rather keep yourself, I understand, and I will vote approve for Theo, Priya, and Sam. I will not spend a rejection on the third slot, because every team available to us contains an Evil player and a rejection does not change that.

Isha, I understand your preference to include yourself, but I am keeping Theo, Priya, and Sam. Like you, I can trust my own card, and Theo and Priya have a successful mission together, even if that result is not proof of their alignment.

One correction: with three Good players among five, an all-Good three-person team is possible. Also, Noah was vocal on Mission 1; it was Sam who spoke only after being prompted. Neither correction proves anyone's alignment. I still think the proposed team is a reasonable way to build on Mission 1, and I will vote approve.

I'm keeping my position on Theo, Priya, and Sam. Noah, your alternative of Theo, Isha, and yourself asks the table to trust a seat you have wanted since Mission 1. That is the same kind of unverified risk you attribute to the current team. Every three-person team carries the single-Fail exposure you describe, so the useful question is who has behaved consistently. Mission 1 succeeded with Theo and me on the team, and no one has produced a concrete fact against either of us. Isha's point that a fail would have been more informative is fair, but a success is still a real data point, and rejecting this team would only pass leadership without adding evidence. I'll vote approve, and I ask the table to judge all three of us on what Mission 2 shows.

I will vote approve for Theo, Priya, and Sam. I know my own card is Good, and Mission 1 succeeded with Theo and Priya. That is not proof of Priya, but it is the only mission result we have. Sam's self-inclusion is a fair concern, and I do not treat it as proof of Evil; every three-person proposal here rests on judgment. A rejection would pass leadership to Noah, whose proposed Theo, Isha, Noah team is not demonstrably safer and whose case has relied on a standard that his own alternative cannot meet. I also note Isha's claim that Noah was nearly silent in Mission 1 is not supported by the record: Noah spoke several times before Sam's first statement. That does not prove alignment, but it weakens the conduct-based argument against this team. I will approve so Mission 2 resolves and gives us real information; if it fails, the table should read the result with the votes and behavior of all three members.

Two corrections on the record before I close, because both were mine to own.

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
